entries.1deca088f3ff25b538657f4d6ba2d7e38d9d7f05: <div sID="gen8876" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="9" osisID="Neh.9" sID="Neh.9"/> <div eID="gen8876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8877" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen8878" type="x-p"/> The tenth day of the seventh month between the feast of trumpets (<reference osisRef="Neh.8.2">ch. viii. 2</reference>) and the feast of tabernacles (<reference osisRef="Neh.9.14">ver. 14</reference>) was appointed to be the day of atonement; we have no reason to think but that it was religiously observed, though it is not mentioned. But here we have an account of an occasional fast that was kept a fortnight after that, with reference to the present posture of their affairs, and it was, as that, a day of humiliation. There is a time to weep as well as a time to laugh. We have here an account. I. How this fast was observed, <reference osisRef="Neh.9.1-Neh.9.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. What were the heads of the prayer that was made to God on that occasion, wherein they made a thankful acknowledgment of God's mercies, a penitent confession of sin, and a humble submission to the righteous hand of God in the judgments that were brought upon them, concluding with a solemn resolution of new obedience, <reference osisRef="Neh.9.4-Neh.9.38">ver. 4-38</reference>.
entries.db0048444b6754def292a874119a70dd721a157e: <div eID="gen8878" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen8877" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Repentance of the People. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 444.)</title> <div sID="gen8879" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now in the twenty and fourth day of this month the children of Israel were assembled with fasting, and with sackclothes, and earth upon them. <hi type="super">2</hi> And the seed of Israel separated themselves from all strangers, and stood and confessed their sins, and the iniquities of their fathers. <hi type="super">3</hi> And they stood up in their place, and read in the book of the law of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> their God <hi type="italic">one</hi> fourth part of the day; and <hi type="italic">another</hi> fourth part they confessed, and worshipped the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> their God. <div eID="gen8879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8880" type="x-p"/> We have here a general account of a public fast which the children of Israel kept, probably by order from Nehemiah, by and with the advice and consent of the chief of the fathers. It was a fast that men appointed, but such <hi type="italic">a fast as God had chosen;</hi> for, 1. It was a day <hi type="italic">to afflict the soul,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.58.5">Isa. lviii. 5</reference>. Probably they assembled in the courts of the temple, and they there appeared in sackcloth and in the posture of mourners, with earth on their heads, <reference osisRef="Neh.9.1">v. 1</reference>. By these outward expressions of sorrow and humiliation they gave glory to God, took shame to themselves, and stirred up one another to repentance. They were restrained from <hi type="italic">weeping,</hi> <reference osisRef="Neh.8.9">ch. viii. 9</reference>, but now they were directed to weep. The joy of our holy feasts must give way to the sorrow of our solemn fasts when they come. Every thing is beautiful in its season. 2. It was a day <hi type="italic">to loose the bands of wickedness,</hi> and that is the fast that God has chosen, <reference osisRef="Isa.58.6">Isa. lviii. 6</reference>. Without this, spreading sackcloth and ashes under us is but a jest. The seed of Israel, because they were a holy seed, appropriated to God and more excellent than their neighbours, <hi type="italic">separated themselves from all strangers</hi> with whom they had mingled and joined in affinity, <reference osisRef="Neh.9.2">v. 2</reference>. Ezra had separated them from their strange wives some years before, but they had relapsed into the same sin, and had either made marriages or at least made friendships with them, and contracted such an intimacy as was a snare to them. But now they separated themselves from the strange children as well as from the strange wives. Those that intend by prayers and covenants to join themselves to God must separate themselves from sin and sinners; for <hi type="italic">what communion hath light with darkness?</hi> 3. It was a day of communion with God. <hi type="italic">They fasted to him, even to him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zech.7.5">Zech. vii. 5</reference>); for, (1.) They spoke to him in prayer, offered their pious and devout affections to him in the confession of sin and the adoration of him as the Lord and their God. Fasting without prayer is a body without a soul, a worthless carcase. (2.) They heard him speaking to them by his word; for they read in the book of the law, which is very proper on fasting days, that, in the glass of the law, we may see our deformities and defilements, and know what to acknowledge and what to amend. The word will direct and quicken prayer, for by it the Spirit helps our praying infirmities. Observe how the time was equally divided between these two. Three hours (for that is the fourth part of a day) they spent in reading, expounding, and applying the scriptures, and three hours in confessing sin and praying; so that they staid together six hours, and spent all the time in the solemn acts of religion, without saying, <hi type="italic">Behold, what a weariness is it!</hi> The varying of the exercises made it the less tedious, and, as the word they read would furnish them with matter for prayer, so prayer would make the word the more profitable. Bishop Patrick thinks that they spent the whole twelve hours of the day in devotion, that from six o'clock in the morning till nine they read, and then from nine to twelve they prayed, from twelve to three they read again, and from three till six at night they prayed again. The word of a fast day is good work, and therefore we should endeavour to make a day's work, a good day's work, of it.
entries.0ea6b96d6d461301b116b055af95c3937d7c91d1: <div eID="gen8880" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Prayer of the Levites. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 444.)</title> <div sID="gen8881" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> Then stood up upon the stairs, of the Levites, Jeshua, and Bani, Kadmiel, Shebaniah, Bunni, Sherebiah, Bani, <hi type="italic">and</hi> Chenani, and cried with a loud voice unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> their God. <hi type="super">5</hi> Then the Levites, Jeshua, and Kadmiel, Bani, Hashabniah, Sherebiah, Hodijah, Shebaniah, <hi type="italic">and</hi> Pethahiah, said, Stand up <hi type="italic">and</hi> bless the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God for ever and ever: and blessed be thy glorious name, which is exalted above all blessing and praise. <hi type="super">6</hi> Thou, <hi type="italic">even</hi> thou, <hi type="italic">art</hi> <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> alone; thou hast made heaven, the heaven of heavens, with all their host, the earth, and all <hi type="italic">things</hi> that <hi type="italic">are</hi> therein, the seas, and all that <hi type="italic">is</hi> therein, and thou preservest them all; and the host of heaven worshippeth thee. <hi type="super">7</hi> Thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> the God, who didst choose Abram, and broughtest him forth out of Ur of the Chaldees, and gavest him the name of Abraham; <hi type="super">8</hi> And foundest his heart faithful before thee, and madest a covenant with him to give the land of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, and the Perizzites, and the Jebusites, and the Girgashites, to give <hi type="italic">it, I say,</hi> to his seed, and hast performed thy words; for thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> righteous: <hi type="super">9</hi> And didst see the affliction of our fathers in Egypt, and heardest their cry by the Red sea; <hi type="super">10</hi> And showedst signs and wonders upon Pharaoh, and on all his servants, and on all the people of his land: for thou knewest that they dealt proudly against them. So didst thou get thee a name, as <hi type="italic">it is</hi> this day. <hi type="super">11</hi> And thou didst divide the sea before them, so that they went through the midst of the sea on the dry land; and their persecutors thou threwest into the deeps, as a stone into the mighty waters. <hi type="super">12</hi> Moreover thou leddest them in the day by a cloudy pillar; and in the night by a pillar of fire, to give them light in the way wherein they should go. <hi type="super">13</hi> Thou camest down also upon mount Sinai, and spakest with them from heaven, and gavest them right judgments, and true laws, good statutes and commandments: <hi type="super">14</hi> And madest known unto them thy holy sabbath, and commandedst them precepts, statutes, and laws, by the hand of Moses thy servant: <hi type="super">15</hi> And gavest them bread from heaven for their hunger, and broughtest forth water for them out of the rock for their thirst, and promisedst them that they should go in to possess the land which thou hadst sworn to give them. <hi type="super">16</hi> But they and our fathers dealt proudly, and hardened their necks, and hearkened not to thy commandments, <hi type="super">17</hi> And refused to obey, neither were mindful of thy wonders that thou didst among them; but hardened their necks, and in their rebellion appointed a captain to return to their bondage: but thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> a God ready to pardon, gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and forsookest them not. <hi type="super">18</hi> Yea, when they had made them a molten calf, and said, This <hi type="italic">is</hi> thy God that brought thee up out of Egypt, and had wrought great provocations; <hi type="super">19</hi> Yet thou in thy manifold mercies forsookest them not in the wilderness: the pillar of the cloud departed not from them by day, to lead them in the way; neither the pillar of fire by night, to show them light, and the way wherein they should go. <hi type="super">20</hi> Thou gavest also thy good spirit to instruct them, and withheldest not thy manna from their mouth, and gavest them water for their thirst. <hi type="super">21</hi> Yea, forty years didst thou sustain them in the wilderness, <hi type="italic">so that</hi> they lacked nothing; their clothes waxed not old, and their feet swelled not. <hi type="super">22</hi> Moreover thou gavest them kingdoms and nations, and didst divide them into corners: so they possessed the land of Sihon, and the land of the king of Heshbon, and the land of Og king of Bashan. <hi type="super">23</hi> Their children also multipliedst thou as the stars of heaven, and broughtest them into the land, concerning which thou hadst promised to their fathers, that they should go in to possess <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <hi type="super">24</hi> So the children went in and possessed the land, and thou subduedst before them the inhabitants of the land, the Canaanites, and gavest them into their hands, with their kings, and the people of the land, that they might do with them as they would. <hi type="super">25</hi> And they took strong cities, and a fat land, and possessed houses full of all goods, wells digged, vineyards, and oliveyards, and fruit trees in abundance: so they did eat, and were filled, and became fat, and delighted themselves in thy great goodness. <hi type="super">26</hi> Nevertheless they were disobedient, and rebelled against thee, and cast thy law behind their backs, and slew thy prophets which testified against them to turn them to thee, and they wrought great provocations. <hi type="super">27</hi> Therefore thou deliveredst them into the hand of their enemies, who vexed them: and in the time of their trouble, when they cried unto thee, thou heardest <hi type="italic">them</hi> from heaven; and according to thy manifold mercies thou gavest them saviours, who saved them out of the hand of their enemies. <hi type="super">28</hi> But after they had rest, they did evil again before thee: therefore leftest thou them in the hand of their enemies, so that they had the dominion over them: yet when they returned, and cried unto thee, thou heardest <hi type="italic">them</hi> from heaven; and many times didst thou deliver them according to thy mercies; <hi type="super">29</hi> And testifiedst against them, that thou mightest bring them again unto thy law: yet they dealt proudly, and hearkened not unto thy commandments, but sinned against thy judgments, (which if a man do, he shall live in them;) and withdrew the shoulder, and hardened their neck, and would not hear. <hi type="super">30</hi> Yet many years didst thou forbear them, and testifiedst against them by thy spirit in thy prophets: yet would they not give ear: therefore gavest thou them into the hand of the people of the lands. <hi type="super">31</hi> Nevertheless for thy great mercies' sake thou didst not utterly consume them, nor forsake them; for thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> a gracious and merciful God. <hi type="super">32</hi> Now therefore, our God, the great, the mighty, and the terrible God, who keepest covenant and mercy, let not all the trouble seem little before thee, that hath come upon us, on our kings, on our princes, and on our priests, and on our prophets, and on our fathers, and on all thy people, since the time of the kings of Assyria unto this day. <hi type="super">33</hi> Howbeit thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> just in all that is brought upon us; for thou hast done right, but we have done wickedly: <hi type="super">34</hi> Neither have our kings, our princes, our priests, nor our fathers, kept thy law, nor hearkened unto thy commandments and thy testimonies, wherewith thou didst testify against them. <hi type="super">35</hi> For they have not served thee in their kingdom, and in thy great goodness that thou gavest them, and in the large and fat land which thou gavest before them, neither turned they from their wicked works. <hi type="super">36</hi> Behold, we <hi type="italic">are</hi> servants this day, and <hi type="italic">for</hi> the land that thou gavest unto our fathers to eat the fruit thereof and the good thereof, behold, we <hi type="italic">are</hi> servants in it: <hi type="super">37</hi> And it yieldeth much increase unto the kings whom thou hast set over us because of our sins: also they have dominion over our bodies, and over our cattle, at their pleasure, and we <hi type="italic">are</hi> in great distress. <hi type="super">38</hi> And because of all this we make a sure <hi type="italic">covenant,</hi> and write <hi type="italic">it;</hi> and our princes, Levites, <hi type="italic">and</hi> priests, seal <hi type="italic">unto it.</hi> <div eID="gen8881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8882" type="x-p"/> We have here an account how the work of this fast-day was carried on. 1. The names of the ministers that were employed. They are twice named (<reference osisRef="Neh.9.4-Neh.9.5">v. 4, 5</reference>), only with some variation of the names. Either they prayed successively, according to that rule which the apostle gives (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.31">1 Cor. xiv. 31</reference>, <hi type="italic">You may all prophesy one by one</hi>), or, as some think, there were eight several congregations at some distance from each other, and each had a Levite to preside in it. 2. The work itself in which they employed themselves. (1.) They prayed to God, cried to him with a loud voice (<reference osisRef="Neh.9.4">v. 4</reference>), for the pardon of the sins of Israel and God's favour to them. They cried aloud, not that God might the better hear them, as Baal's worshippers, but that the people might, and to excite their fervency. (2.) They praised God; for the work of praise is not unseasonable on a fast-day; in all acts of devotion we must aim at this, to <hi type="italic">give unto God the glory due to his name.</hi> The summary of their prayers we have here upon record; whether drawn up before, as a directory to the Levites what to enlarge on, or recollected after, as the heads of what they had in prayer enlarged upon, is uncertain. Much more no doubt was said than is here recorded, else confessing and worshipping God would not have taken up a fourth part of the day, much less two-fourths. <div eID="gen8882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8883" type="x-p"/> In this solemn address to God we have, <div eID="gen8883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8884" type="x-p"/> I. An awful adoration of God, as a perfect and glorious Being, and the fountain of all beings, <reference osisRef="Neh.9.5-Neh.9.6">v. 5, 6</reference>. The congregation is called upon to signify their concurrence herewith by standing up; and so the minister directs himself to God, <hi type="italic">Blessed be thy glorious name.</hi> God is here adored, 1. As the only living and true God: <hi type="italic">Thou art Jehovah alone,</hi> self-existent and independent; there is no God besides thee. 2. As the Creator of all things: <hi type="italic">Thou hast made heaven, earth, and seas,</hi> and all that is in them. The first article of our creed is fitly made the first article of our praises. 3. As the great Protector of the whole creation: "Thou preservest in being all the creatures thou hast given being to." God's providence extends itself to the highest beings, for they need it, and to the meanest, for they are not slighted by it. What God has made he will preserve; what he does is done effectually, <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.14">Eccl. iii. 14</reference>. 4. As the object of the creatures' praises: "<hi type="italic">The host of heaven,</hi> the world of holy angels, <hi type="italic">worshippeth thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Neh.9.6">v. 6</reference>. But thy <hi type="italic">name is exalted above all blessing and praise;</hi> it needs not the praises of the creatures, nor is any addition made to its glory by those praises." The best performances in the praising of God's name, even those of the angels themselves, fall infinitely short of what it deserves. It is not only exalted above our blessing, but above all blessing. Put all the praises of heaven and earth together, and the thousandth part is not said of what might and should be said of the glory of God. <hi type="italic">Our goodness extendeth not to him.</hi> <div eID="gen8884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8885" type="x-p"/> II. A thankful acknowledgment of God's favours to Israel. <div eID="gen8885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8886" type="x-p"/> 1. Many of these are here reckoned up in order before him, and very much to the purpose, for, (1.) We must take all occasions to mention the loving kindness of the Lord, and <hi type="italic">in every prayer give thanks.</hi> (2.) When we are confessing our sins it is good to take notice of the mercies of God as the aggravations of our sins, that we may be the more humbled and ashamed, and call ourselves by the scandalous name of ungrateful. (3.) When we are seeking to God for mercy and relief in the time of distress it is an encouragement to our faith and hope to look back upon our own and our fathers' experiences: "Lord, thou hast done well for us formerly; shall it be all undone again? Art not thou the same God still?" <div eID="gen8886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8887" type="x-p"/> 2. Let us briefly observe the particular instances of God's goodness to Israel here recounted. (1.) The call of Abraham, <reference osisRef="Neh.9.7">v. 7</reference>. God's favour to him was distinguishing: "Thou didst choose him." His grace in him was powerful to bring him out of Ur of the Chaldees, and, in giving him the name of Abraham, he put honour upon him as his own and assured him that he should be the <hi type="italic">father of many nations. Look unto Abraham your father</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.51.2">Isa. li. 2</reference>) and see free grace glorified in him. (2.) The covenant God made with him to give the land of Canaan to him and his seed, a type of the better country, <reference osisRef="Neh.9.8">v. 8</reference>. And this covenant was sure, for God found Abraham's heart faithful before God, and found it so because he made it so (for faith is not of ourselves, it is the gift of God), and therefore performed his words; <hi type="italic">for with the upright he will show himself upright,</hi> and wherever he finds a faithful heart he will be found a faithful God. (3.) The deliverance of Israel out of Egypt, <reference osisRef="Neh.9.9-Neh.9.11">v. 9-11</reference>. It was seasonable to remember this now that they were interceding for the perfecting of their deliverance out of Babylon. They were then delivered, in compassion to their affliction, in answer to their cry, and in resistance of the pride and insolence of their persecutors. Wherein they dealt proudly, God showed himself <hi type="italic">above them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.18.11">Exod. xviii. 11</reference>), and so got himself <hi type="italic">a name;</hi> for he said, <hi type="italic">I will get me honour upon Pharaoh.</hi> Even to this day the name of God is glorified for that wonderful work. It was done miraculously: signs and wonders were shown for the effecting of it; their deliverance was the destruction of their enemies; they were <hi type="italic">thrown into the deeps,</hi> as irrecoverably <hi type="italic">as a stone into the mighty waters.</hi> (4.) The conducting of them through the wilderness, by the pillar of cloud and fire, which showed them which way they should go, when they should remove, and when and where they should rest, directed all their stages and all their steps, <reference osisRef="Neh.9.12">v. 12</reference>. It was also a visible token of God's presence with them, to guide and guard them. They mention this again (<reference osisRef="Neh.9.19">v. 19</reference>), observing that though they had by their sins provoked God to withdraw from them, and leave them to wander and perish in the by-paths of the wilderness, yet in his manifold mercy he continued to lead them, and took not away the <hi type="italic">pillar of cloud and fire,</hi> <reference osisRef="Neh.9.19">v. 19</reference>. When mercies, though forfeited, are continued, we are bound to be doubly thankful. (5.) The plentiful provision made for them in the wilderness, that they might not perish for hunger: Thou <hi type="italic">gavest them bread from heaven,</hi> and <hi type="italic">water out of the rock</hi> (<reference osisRef="Neh.9.15">v. 15</reference>), and, to hold up their hearts, a promise that they should go in and possess the land of Canaan. They had meat and drink, food convenient in the way, and the good land at their journey's end; what would they more? This also is repeated (<reference osisRef="Neh.9.20">v. 20, 21</reference>) as that which was continued, notwithstanding their provocations: <hi type="italic">Forty years didst thou sustain them.</hi> Never was people so long nursed and so tenderly; they were wonderfully provided for, and, in so long a time, <hi type="italic">their clothes waxed not old,</hi> and, though the way was rough and tedious, <hi type="italic">their feet swelled not;</hi> for they were <hi type="italic">carried as upon eagles' wings.</hi> (6.) The giving of the law upon Mount Sinai. This was the greatest favour of all that was done them and the greatest honour that was put upon them. The Lawgiver was very glorious, <reference osisRef="Neh.9.13">v. 13</reference>. "Thou didst not only send, but camest down thyself, and <hi type="italic">didst speak with them,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Deut.4.33">Deut. iv. 33</reference>. The law given was very good. No nation under the sun had such <hi type="italic">right judgments, true laws,</hi> and <hi type="italic">good statutes,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.4.8">Deut. iv. 8</reference>. The moral and judicial precepts were true and right, founded upon natural equity and the eternal reasons of good and evil; and even the ceremonial institutions were good, tokens of God's goodness to them and types of gospel grace. Particular notice is taken of the law of the fourth commandment as a great favour to them: <hi type="italic">Thou madest known unto them thy holy sabbath,</hi> which was a token of God's particular favour to them, distinguishing them from the nations who had revolted from God and quite lost that ancient part of revealed religion, and was likewise a means of keeping up their communion with him. And, with <hi type="italic">the law</hi> and <hi type="italic">the sabbath,</hi> he <hi type="italic">gave his good Spirit to instruct them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Neh.9.20">v. 20</reference>. Besides the law given on Mount Sinai, the five books of Moses, which he wrote <hi type="italic">as he was moved by the Holy Ghost,</hi> were constant instructions to them, particularly the book of Deuteronomy, in which God's Spirit by Moses instructed them fully. Bezaleel was filled <hi type="italic">with the Spirit of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.31.3">Exod. xxxi. 3</reference>), so was Joshua (<reference osisRef="Num.27.18">Num. xxvii. 18</reference>), and Caleb had another spirit. (7.) The putting of them in possession of Canaan, that good land, <hi type="italic">kingdoms and nations,</hi> <reference osisRef="Neh.9.22">v. 22</reference>. They were made so numerous as to replenish it (<reference osisRef="Neh.9.23">v. 23</reference>) and so victorious as to be masters of it (<reference osisRef="Neh.9.24">v. 24</reference>); the natives were given into their hands, <hi type="italic">that they might do with them as they would,</hi> set their feet, if they pleased, on the necks of their kings. Thus they gained a happy <hi type="italic">settlement,</hi> <reference osisRef="Neh.9.25">v. 25</reference>. Look upon their cities, and you see them strong and well fortified. Look into their houses, and you find them fine and well furnished, filled with all sorts of rich goods. Take a view of the country, and you will say that you never saw such a fat land, so well stored with <hi type="italic">vineyards and oliveyards.</hi> All these they found made ready to their hands; so they delighted themselves in the gifts of God's great goodness. They could not wish to be more easy or happy than they were, or might have been, in Canaan, had it not been their own fault. (8.) God's great readiness to pardon their sins, and work deliverance for them, when they had by their provocations brought his judgments upon themselves. When they were in the wilderness they found him <hi type="italic">a God ready to pardon</hi> (<reference osisRef="Neh.9.17">v. 17</reference>), a <hi type="italic">God of pardons</hi> (so the margin reads it), who had proclaimed his name as a God <hi type="italic">forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin,</hi> who has power to forgive sin, is willing to forgive, and glories in forgiving. Though they forsook him, he did not forsake them, as justly he might have done, but continued his care of them and favour to them. Afterwards, when they were settled in Canaan and sold themselves by their sins into the hands of their enemies, upon their submission and humble request he <hi type="italic">gave them saviours</hi> (<reference osisRef="Neh.9.27">v. 27</reference>), the judges, by whom God wrought many a great deliverance for them when they were on the brink of ruin. This he did, not for any merit of theirs, for their deserved nothing but ill, but according to his mercies, his manifold mercies. (9.) The admonitions and fair warnings he gave them by his servants the prophets. When he delivered them from their troubles he <hi type="italic">testified against their sins</hi> (<reference osisRef="Neh.9.28-Neh.9.29">v. 28, 29</reference>), that they might not misconstrue their deliverances as connivances at their wickedness. That which was designed in all the testimonies which the prophets bore against them was to bring them again to God's law, to lay their necks under its yoke, and walk by its rule. The end of our ministry is to bring people to God by bringing them to his law, not to bring them to ourselves by bringing them under any law of ours. This we have again (<reference osisRef="Neh.9.30">v. 30</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou testifiedst against them by thy Spirit in thy prophets.</hi> The testimony of the prophets was the testimony of the Spirit in the prophets, and it was the Spirit of Christ in them, <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.10-1Pet.1.11">1 Pet. i. 10, 11</reference>. They <hi type="italic">spoke as they were moved by the Holy Ghost,</hi> and what they said is to be received accordingly. God gave them <hi type="italic">his Spirit to instruct them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Neh.9.20">v. 20</reference>), but, they not receiving that instruction, he did by his Spirit testify against them. If we will not suffer God's word to teach and rule us, it will accuse and judge us. God sends prophets, in compassion to his people (<reference osisRef="2Chr.36.15">2 Chron. xxxvi. 15</reference>), that he may not send judgments. (10.) The lengthening out of his patience and the moderating of his rebukes: <hi type="italic">Many years did he forbear them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Neh.9.30">v. 30</reference>), as loth to punish them, and waiting to see if they would repent; and, when he did punish them, he did not <hi type="italic">utterly consume them nor forsake them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Neh.9.31">v. 31</reference>. Had he forsaken them they would have been utterly consumed; but he did not stir up all his wrath, for he designed their reformation, not their destruction. Thus do they multiply, thus do they magnify, the instances of God's goodness to Israel, and we should do in like manner, that the goodness of God, duly considered by us, may lead us to repentance, and overcome our badness. The more thankful we are for God's mercies the more humbled we shall be for our own sins. <div eID="gen8887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8888" type="x-p"/> III. Here is a penitent confession of sin, their own sins, and the sins of their fathers. The mention of these is interwoven with the memorials of God's favours, that God's goodness, notwithstanding their provocations, might appear the more illustrious, and their sins, notwithstanding his favours, might appear the more heinous. Many passages in this acknowledgment of sins and mercies are taken from <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.5-Ezek.20.26 Neh.9.4-Neh.9.38">Ezek. xx. 5-26</reference>, as will appear by comparing those verses with these; for the word of God is of use to direct us in prayer, and by what he says to us we may learn what to say to him. <div eID="gen8888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8889" type="x-p"/> 1. They begin with the sins of Israel in the wilderness: <hi type="italic">They, even our fathers</hi> (so it might better be read), <hi type="italic">dealt proudly</hi> (though, considering what they were, and how lately they had come out of slavery, they had no reason to be proud), <hi type="italic">and hardened their necks,</hi> <reference osisRef="Neh.9.16">v. 16</reference>. Pride is at the bottom of men's obstinacy and disobedience; they think it below them to bow their necks to God's yoke, and a piece of state to set up their own will in opposition to the will of God himself. (1.) There were two things which they did not duly give heed to, else they would not have done as they did:—The word of God they heard, but they did not hearken to God's commandments; and the works of God they saw, but they were not mindful of his wonders: had they duly considered them as miracles, they would have obeyed from a principle of faith and holy fear; had they duly considered them as mercies, they would have obeyed from a principle of gratitude and holy love. But, when men make no right use either of God's ordinances or of his providences, what can be expected from them? (2.) Two great sins are here specified; which they were guilty of in the wilderness—meditating a return, [1.] To Egyptian slavery, which, for the sake of the garlick and onions, they preferred before the glorious liberty of the Israel of God attended with some difficulty and inconvenience. <hi type="italic">In their rebellion they appointed a captain to return to their bondage,</hi> in distrust of God's power and contempt of his holy promise, <reference osisRef="Neh.9.17">v. 17</reference>. [2.] To Egyptian idolatry: <hi type="italic">They made a molten calf,</hi> and were so sottish as to say, <hi type="italic">This is thy God.</hi> <div eID="gen8889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8890" type="x-p"/> 2. They next bewail the provocations of their fathers after they were put in possession of Canaan. Though they were <hi type="italic">delighted themselves in God's great goodness,</hi> yet that would not prevail to keep them closely to him; for, <hi type="italic">nevertheless, they were disobedient</hi> (<reference osisRef="Neh.9.26">v. 26</reference>) <hi type="italic">and wrought great provocations.</hi> For, (1.) They abused God's prophets, <hi type="italic">slew them</hi> because they <hi type="italic">testified against them to turn them to God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Neh.9.26">v. 26</reference>), so returning the greatest injury for the greatest kindness. (2.) They abused his favours: <hi type="italic">After they had rest,</hi> they <hi type="italic">did evil again,</hi> <reference osisRef="Neh.9.28">v. 28</reference>. They were not wrought upon either by their troubles or their deliverances out of trouble. Neither fear nor love would hold them to their duty. <div eID="gen8890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8891" type="x-p"/> 3. They at length come nearer to their own day, and lament the sins which had brought those judgments upon them which they had long been groaning under and were now but in part delivered from: <hi type="italic">We have done wickedly</hi> (<reference osisRef="Neh.9.33">v. 33</reference>): <hi type="italic">our kings, our princes, our priests, and our fathers,</hi> have all been guilty, and we in them, <reference osisRef="Neh.9.34">v. 34</reference>. Two things they charge upon themselves and their fathers, as the cause of their troubles:—(1.) A contempt of the good law God had given them: They <hi type="italic">sinned against thy judgments,</hi> the dictates of divine wisdom, and the demands of divine sovereignty. Though they were told how much it would be for their own advantage to govern themselves by them, for, <hi type="italic">if a man do them, he shall live in them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Neh.9.29">v. 29</reference>), yet they would not do them, and so, in effect, said that they <hi type="italic">would not live.</hi> They <hi type="italic">forsook their own mercies.</hi> This abridgment of the covenant, <hi type="italic">Do this and live,</hi> is taken from <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.13">Ezek. xx. 13</reference>, and is quoted, <reference osisRef="Gal.3.12">Gal. iii. 12</reference>, to prove that <hi type="italic">the law is not of faith;</hi> it was not them as it is now, <hi type="italic">Believe and live,</hi> yet <hi type="italic">they gave a withdrawing shoulder,</hi> so it is in the margin. They pretended to lay their shoulders under the burden of God's law, and put their shoulders to the work, but they proved withdrawing shoulders; they soon flew off, would not keep to it, would not abide by it. When it came, as we say, to the setting to, they shrunk back, and would not hear. They had a backsliding heart; and, though God by his prophets called them to return, they <hi type="italic">would not give ear,</hi> <reference osisRef="Neh.9.30">v. 30</reference>. He <hi type="italic">stretched out his hands, but no man regarded.</hi> (2.) A contempt of the good land God had given them (<reference osisRef="Neh.9.35">v. 35</reference>): "Our kings have <hi type="italic">not served thee in their kingdom,</hi> have not used their power for the support of religion; our people have not served thee in the use of the gifts of thy great goodness, and in that large and fat land which thou not only gavest them by thy grant, but gavest before them by the expulsion of the natives and the complete victories they obtained over them." Those that would not serve God in their own land were made to serve their enemies in a strange land, as was threatened, <reference osisRef="Deut.28.47-Deut.28.48">Deut. xxviii. 47, 48</reference>. It is a pity that a good land should have bad inhabitants, but so it was with Sodom. Fatness and fulness often make men proud and sensual. <div eID="gen8891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8892" type="x-p"/> IV. Here is a humble representation of the judgments of God, which they had been and were now under. <div eID="gen8892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8893" type="x-p"/> 1. Former judgments are remembered as aggravations of their sins, that they had not taken warning. In the days of the judges their <hi type="italic">enemies vexed them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Neh.9.27">v. 27</reference>); and, when they did evil again, God did again <hi type="italic">leave them in the hand of their enemies,</hi> who could not have touched them if God had not given them up; but, when God left them, they got and kept dominion over them. <div eID="gen8893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8894" type="x-p"/> 2. Their present calamitous state is laid before the Lord (<reference osisRef="Neh.9.36-Neh.9.37">v. 36, 37</reference>): <hi type="italic">We are servants this day.</hi> Free-born Israelites are enslaved, and the land which they had long held by a much more honourable tenure than grand sergeantry itself, even by immediate grant from the crown of heaven to them as a peculiar people above all people on the earth, they now held by as base a tenure as villenage itself, by, from, and under, the kings of Persia, whose vassals they were. A sad change! But see what work sin makes! They were bound to personal service: They have <hi type="italic">dominion over our bodies;</hi> they held all they had precariously, were tenants at will, and the land-tax that they paid was so great that it amounted even to a rack-rent; so that all the rents, issues, and profits, of their land did in effect accrue to the king, and it was as much as they could do to get a bare subsistence for themselves and their families out of it. This, they honestly own, was for their sins. Poverty and slavery are the fruits of sin; it is sin that brings us into all our distresses. <div eID="gen8894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8895" type="x-p"/> V. Here is their address to God under these calamities. 1. By way of request, that their trouble might not <hi type="italic">seem little,</hi> <reference osisRef="Neh.9.32">v. 32</reference>. It is the only petition in all this prayer. The trouble was universal; it had come on their <hi type="italic">kings, princes, priests, prophets, fathers, and all their people;</hi> they had all shared in the sin (<reference osisRef="Neh.9.34">v. 34</reference>), and now all shared in the judgment. It was of long continuance: <hi type="italic">From the time of the kings of Assyria,</hi> who carried the ten tribes captive, <hi type="italic">unto this day.</hi> "Lord, let it not all seem little and not worthy to be regarded, or not needing to be relieved." They do not prescribe to God what he shall do for them, but leave it to him, only desiring he would please to take cognizance of it, remembering that when he saw the affliction of his people in Egypt to be great he came down to deliver them, <reference osisRef="Exod.3.7-Exod.3.8">Exod. iii. 7, 8</reference>. In this request they have an eye to God as one that is to be feared (for he is <hi type="italic">the great, the mighty, and the terrible, God</hi>), and as one that is to be trusted, for he is <hi type="italic">our God</hi> in covenant, and a God that <hi type="italic">keeps covenant and mercy.</hi> 2. By way of acknowledgment, notwithstanding, that really it was less than they deserved, <reference osisRef="Neh.9.33">v. 33</reference>. They own the justice of God in all their troubles, that he had done them no wrong. "We have done wickedly in breaking thy laws, and therefore thou hast done right in bringing all these miseries upon us." Note, It becomes us, when we are under the rebukes of divine Providence, though ever so sharp and ever so long, to justify God and to judge ourselves; for he will be <hi type="italic">clear when he judgeth.</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.51.4">Ps. li. 4</reference>. <div eID="gen8895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8896" type="x-p"/> VI. Here is the result and conclusion of this whole matter. After this long remonstrance of their case was made they came at last to this resolution, that they would return to God and to their duty, and oblige themselves never to forsake God, but always to continue in their duty. "Because of all this, we make a sure covenant with God; in consideration of our frequent departures from God, we will now more firmly than ever bind ourselves to him. Because we have smarted so much for sin, we will now stedfastly resolve against it, that we may not any more withdraw the shoulder." Observe, 1. This covenant was made with serious consideration. It is the result of a chain of suitable thoughts, and so is a reasonable service. 2. With great solemnity. It was written, <hi type="italic">in perpetuam rei memoriam—that it might remain a memorial for all ages;</hi> it was sealed and left upon record, that it might be a witness against them if they dealt deceitfully. 3. With joint consent: "<hi type="italic">We make</hi> it; we are all agreed in making it, and do it unanimously, that we may strengthen the hands one of another." 4. With fixed resolution: "It is <hi type="italic">a sure covenant,</hi> without reserving a power of revocation. It is what we will live and die by, and never go back from." A certain number of the princes, priests, and Levites, were chosen as the representatives of the congregation, to subscribe and seal it for and in the name of the rest. Now was fulfilled that promise concerning the Jews, that, when they returned out of captivity, they should <hi type="italic">join themselves to the Lord in a perpetual covenant</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.5">Jer. l. 5</reference>), and that in <reference osisRef="Isa.44.5">Isa. xliv. 5</reference>, that they should <hi type="italic">subscribe with their hand unto the Lord.</hi> He that bears an honest mind will not startle at assurances; nor will those that know the deceitfulness of their own hearts think them needless.  <chapter eID="Neh.9"/> <div eID="gen8896" type="x-p"/>

entries.108d85de4e05a628f382d15c12ae9b8f8d4dd104: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4349"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 9</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Neh.9.1-Neh.9.3">Ne 9:1-3</reference>. A Solemn Fast and Repentance of the People.</title> <div sID="gen6299" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4349"/><hi type="bold">1. Now in the twenty and fourth day of this month--</hi>that is, on the second day after the close of the feast of tabernacles, which commenced on the fourteenth and terminated on the twenty-second (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.34-Lev.23.37">Le 23:34-37</reference>). The day immediately after that feast, the twenty-third, had been occupied in separating the delinquents from their unlawful wives, as well, perhaps, as in taking steps for keeping aloof in future from unnecessary intercourse with the heathen around them. For although this necessary measure of reformation had been begun formerly by Ezra (<reference osisRef="Ezra.10.1-Ezra.10.17">Ezr 10:1-17</reference>), and satisfactorily accomplished at that time (in so far as he had information of the existing abuses, or possessed the power of correcting them) yet it appears that this reformatory work of Ezra had been only partial and imperfect. Many cases of delinquency had escaped, or new defaulters had appeared who had contracted those forbidden alliances; and there was an urgent necessity for Nehemiah again to take vigorous measures for the removal of a social evil which threatened the most disastrous consequences to the character and prosperity of the chosen people. A solemn fast was now observed for the expression of those penitential and sorrowful feelings which the reading of the law had produced, but which had been suppressed during the celebration of the feast; and the sincerity of their repentance was evinced by the decisive steps taken for the correction of existing abuses in the matter of marriage. <div eID="gen6299" type="x-p"/>
entries.54c4722be1552e5d62af9a16adf44f7262053aa6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4350"/><div sID="gen6300" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4350"/><hi type="bold">2. confessed their sins, and the iniquities of their fathers--</hi>Not only did they read in their recent sufferings a punishment of the national apostasy and guilt, but they had made themselves partakers of their fathers' sins by following the same evil ways. <div eID="gen6300" type="x-p"/>
entries.c1fdc2edc5215cf2a6c3f8d0b621c52dc4667bac: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4351"/><div sID="gen6301" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4351"/><hi type="bold">3. they ... read in the book of the law--</hi>Their extraordinary zeal led them to continue this as before.<div eID="gen6301" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6302" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">one fourth part of the day--</hi>that is, for three hours, twelve hours being the acknowledged length of the Jewish day (<reference osisRef="John.11.9">Joh 11:9</reference>). This solemn diet of worship, which probably commenced at the morning sacrifice, was continued for six hours, that is, till the time of the evening sacrifice. The worship which they gave to the Lord their God, at this season of solemn national humiliation, consisted in acknowledging and adoring His great mercy in the forgiveness of their great and multiplied offenses, in delivering them from the merited judgments which they had already experienced or which they had reason to apprehend, in continuing amongst them the light and blessings of His word and worship, and in supplicating the extension of His grace and protection. <div eID="gen6302" type="x-p"/>
entries.43c7e9d49fc6686cd9fb0914192962a2305b8132: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4352"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Neh.9.4-Neh.9.38">Ne 9:4-38</reference>. The Levites Confess God's Manifold Goodness, and Their Own Wickedness.</title> <div sID="gen6303" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4352"/><hi type="bold">4. Then stood up upon the stairs--</hi>the scaffolds or pulpits, whence the Levites usually addressed the people. There were probably several placed at convenient distances, to prevent confusion and the voice of one drowning those of the others.<div eID="gen6303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6304" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cried with a loud voice unto the Lord--</hi>Such an exertion, of course, was indispensably necessary, in order that the speakers might be heard by the vast multitude congregated in the open air. But these speakers were then engaged in expressing their deep sense of sin, as well as fervently imploring the forgiving mercy of God; and "crying with a loud voice" was a natural accompaniment of this extraordinary prayer meeting, as violent gestures and vehement tones are always the way in which the Jews, and other people in the East, have been accustomed to give utterance to deep and earnest feelings. <div eID="gen6304" type="x-p"/>
entries.4b3bb9653b0769ee9d69cfb2602dddc63bc577a5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4353"/><div sID="gen6305" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4353"/><hi type="bold">5. Then the Levites ... said, Stand up and bless the Lord your God--</hi>If this prayer was uttered by all these Levites in common, it must have been prepared and adopted beforehand, perhaps, by Ezra; but it may only embody the substance of the confession and thanksgiving. <div eID="gen6305" type="x-p"/>
entries.0d2020161c82c27bcf66584d3df6f25ca1176269: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4354"/><div sID="gen6306" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4354"/><hi type="bold">6-38. Thou, even thou, art Lord alone, &c.--</hi>In this solemn and impressive prayer, in which they make public confession of their sins, and deprecate the judgments due to the transgressions of their fathers, they begin with a profound adoration of God, whose supreme majesty and omnipotence is acknowledged in the creation, preservation, and government of all. Then they proceed to enumerate His mercies and distinguished favors to them as a nation, from the period of the call of their great ancestor and the gracious promise intimated to him in the divinely bestowed name of Abraham, a promise which implied that he was to be the Father of the faithful, the ancestor of the Messiah, and the honored individual in whose seed all the families of the earth should be blessed. Tracing in full and minute detail the signal instances of divine interposition for their deliverance and their interest--in their deliverance from Egyptian bondage--their miraculous passage through the Red Sea--the promulgation of His law--the forbearance and long-suffering shown them amid their frequent rebellions--the signal triumphs given them over their enemies--their happy settlement in the promised land--and all the extraordinary blessings, both in the form of temporal prosperity and of religious privilege, with which His paternal goodness had favored them above all other people, they charge themselves with making a miserable requital. They confess their numerous and determined acts of disobedience. They read, in the loss of their national independence and their long captivity, the severe punishment of their sins. They acknowledge that, in all heavy and continued judgments upon their nation, God had done right, but they had done wickedly. And in throwing themselves on His mercy, they express their purpose of entering into a national covenant, by which they pledge themselves to dutiful obedience in future. <div eID="gen6306" type="x-p"/>

entries.3b150bf496f801be36912d68593ec9a493473c97: <div eID="gen15172" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen15173" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15174" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15174" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15173" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15175" type="x-p"/> On the twenty-fourth day of the seventh month, the people hold a solemn fast unto the Lord, and confess their sins, <reference osisRef="Neh.9.1-Neh.9.3">Neh 9:1-3</reference>. The Levites give a general account of God's kindness and forbearance to them and to their fathers; and acknowledge God's mercies and judgments, vv. 4-37. They make a covenant with the Lord, <reference osisRef="Neh.9.38">Neh 9:38</reference>. <div eID="gen15175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15176" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen15176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15177" type="x-p"/> Now in the twenty and fourth day - The feast of trumpets was on the first day of this month; on the fourteenth began the feast of tabernacles, which, lasting seven days, finished on the twenty-second; on the twenty-third they separated themselves from their illegitimate wives and children; and, on the twenty-fourth, they held a solemn day of fasting and confession of sin, and reading the law, which they closed by renewing their covenants.
entries.a31151ffcb5456b9800a230776c91d6e3922b98b: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen15177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15178" type="x-p"/> The seed of Israel separated themselves - A reformation of this kind was begun by Ezra, <reference osisRef="Ezr.10.3">Ezr 10:3</reference>; but it appears that either more were found out who had taken strange wives, or else those who had separated from them had taken them again. <div eID="gen15178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15179" type="x-p"/> And stood and confessed their sins, and the iniquities of their fathers. - They acknowledged that they had been sinners against God throughout all their generations; that their fathers had sinned and were punished; and that they, with this example before their eyes, had copied their fathers' offenses.
entries.4e8cb8031035733c08848950d7d54d57544bcc84: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen15179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15180" type="x-p"/> One fourth part of the day - As they did no manner of work on this day of fasting and humiliation, so they spent the whole of it in religious duties. They began, says Calmet, on the first hour, and continued these exercises to the third hour; from the third they recommenced, and continued till the sixth hour; from the sixth to the ninth; and from the ninth, to the twelfth or last hour. <div eID="gen15180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15181" type="x-p"/> 1. They heard the law read, standing; <div eID="gen15181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15182" type="x-p"/> 2. They prostrated themselves, and confessed their sins; <div eID="gen15182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15183" type="x-p"/> 3. They arose to praise God for having spared and dealt thus mercifully with them.
entries.23f806741efeb3730bdfe0416f822692faf607f7: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen15183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15184" type="x-p"/> Stand up and bless the Lord your God - It is the shameless custom of many congregations of people to sit still while they profess to bless and praise God, by singing the Psalms of David or hymns made on the plan of the Gospel! I ask such persons, Did they ever feel the spirit of devotion while thus employed? If they do, it must be owned that, by the prevalence of habit, they have counteracted the influence of an attitude most friendly to such acts of devotion.
entries.dc5f05aba886379cc6389931a435c7ea59433a55: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen15184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15185" type="x-p"/> Thou preservest them all - ואתה מחיה את כלם vettah mechaiyeh eth cullam, and thou givest life to them all: and the host of the heavens, לך משתחוים lecha mishtachavim, prostrate themselves unto thee. How near is this to the opinion of Kepler, that all the heavenly host are instinct with life, and navigate the great expanse on pinions adjusted to their situation in their respective orbits! But to preserve in life, or in being, is a very good meaning in the original, which does not necessarily imply vitality. We say a tree is alive when flourishing, a plant is dead when it withers, etc.
entries.d0eddbfebf098da284045d9e855bb8069a8dc04e: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen15185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15186" type="x-p"/> Who didst choose Abram - See the notes on <reference osisRef="Exo.13.21">Exo 13:21</reference> (note). <div eID="gen15186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15187" type="x-p"/> The name of Abraham - For the explanation of this name, See the notes on <reference osisRef="Gen.17.5">Gen 17:5</reference>.
entries.7d5aea1b65a3e82f980897a93b8f223927cbcca2: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen15187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15188" type="x-p"/> By a cloudy pillar - See the notes on the parallel passages, both here and in the other verses.
entries.bb43cb4526d78ae64ccbb5d0b1c3acb30cdad7da: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen15188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15189" type="x-p"/> Madest known unto them thy holy Sabbath - They appear to have forgotten this first of all the commandments of God, during their sojourning in Egypt.
entries.5b32b79e0fc29a205fa47fe2a19a03c96eda4029: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen15189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15190" type="x-p"/> And in their rebellion appointed a captain - This clause, read according to its order in the Hebrew text, is thus: And appointed a captain to return to their bondage in their rebellion. But it is probable that במרים bemiryam, in their rebellion, is a mistake for במצרים bemitsrayim, in Egypt. This is the reading of seven of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS., the Neapolitan edition of the Hagiographa, and the Septuagint. It is also the reading in <reference osisRef="Num.14.4">Num 14:4</reference>. The clause should undoubtedly be read, They appointed a captain to return to their bondage in Egypt.
entries.ff3f75cba3ff81c16f317e429fed8ab265f1889b: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen15190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15191" type="x-p"/> The pillar of the cloud departed not from them - מעליהם mealeyhem, "from over them." I have already had occasion to observe that this miraculous cloud, the symbol of the Divine presence, assumed three different positions while accompanying the Israelitish camp: <div eID="gen15191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15192" type="x-p"/> 1. As a cloud in the form of a pillar, it went before them when they journey, to point out their way in the wilderness. <div eID="gen15192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15193" type="x-p"/> 2. As a pillar of fire, it continued with them during the night, to give them light, and be a rallying point for the whole camp in the night season. <div eID="gen15193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15194" type="x-p"/> 3. As an extended cloud, it hovered over them in their encampments, to refresh them with its dews, and to keep them from the ardours of the sun.
entries.dab26ad9a4267840da532b310236b30239476aea: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen15194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15195" type="x-p"/> Their clothes waxed not old - See the note on <reference osisRef="Deu.8.4">Deu 8:4</reference>.
entries.f626ee596bea0fee4faaa3d46980180fa4fad461: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen15195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15196" type="x-p"/> The land of Og king of Bashan - It is most evident that Sihon was king of Heshbon. How then can it be said that they possessed the land of Sihon, and the land of the king of Heshbon? The words the land of the king of Heshbon are wanting in two of De Rossi's MSS. In another MS. the words and the land of are wanting; so that the clause is read, They possessed the land of Sihon, king of Heshbon. The Septuagint has the same reading; the Arabic nearly the same, viz., the land of Sihon, the land of the king of Heshbon. The Syriac has, They possessed the land of Sihon, the land of the Kings of Heshbon. The reading of the text is undoubtedly wrong; that supported by the MSS. and by the Septuagint is most likely to be the true one. Those of the Arabic and Syriac contain at least no contradictory sense. The and in the Hebrew and our version, distinguishes two lands and two kings; the land of Sihon and the land of the king of Heshbon: when it is most certain that only one land and one king can be meant: but the ו vau may be translated here as it often is, even: Even the land of the king of Heshbon.
entries.c080972cb373f3c6219caac2e7ed8ef9c30c5f76: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen15196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15197" type="x-p"/> Became fat, and delighted themselves - They became effeminate, fell under the power of luxury, got totally corrupted in their manners, sinned against all the mercies of God, and then were destroyed by his judgments. We have an old nervous saying, "War begets poverty, poverty begets peace, peace begets affluence, affluence begets luxury and corruption of manners; and hence civil broils, foreign wars, and desolations." A sensible Roman historian has said the same: "Imperium facile iis artibus retinetur, quibus initio partum est: verum ubi pro Labore, Desidia; pro continentia et aequitate, Libido atque Superbia invasere: fortuna simul cum moribus Immutatur."
entries.c9faa9916f7231af7f76e1d465cc6d9bc92c1637: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen15197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15198" type="x-p"/> Thou gavest them saviors - The whole book of Judges is a history of God's mercies, and their rebellions.
entries.f8d7bf06f157966ad1c7f2b1ed803938e3341d76: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen15198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15199" type="x-p"/> Many years didst thou forbear - It is supposed that Nehemiah refers here principally to the ten tribes. And many years did God bear with them; not less than two hundred and fifty-four years from their separation from the house of David, till their captivity and utter dispersion under Shalmaneser; during the whole of which time God invariably warned them by his prophets; or, as it is here said, by thy Spirit in thy prophets, which gives us the true notion of Divine inspiration. God's Spirit was given to the prophets; and they testified to the people, according as they were taught and influenced by this Spirit.
entries.9fb86d18b639b873d9705f49e01d313f18cfa892: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen15199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15200" type="x-p"/> On our kings, on our princes - I believe Nehemiah in this place mentions the whole of civil society in its officers as they stand related to each other in dignity: - <div eID="gen15200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15201" type="x-p"/> 1. Kings, as supreme. <div eID="gen15201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15202" type="x-p"/> 2. Princes. <div eID="gen15202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15203" type="x-p"/> 3. Priests. <div eID="gen15203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15204" type="x-p"/> 4. Prophets. <div eID="gen15204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15205" type="x-p"/> 5. The Fathers, heads or chiefs of tribes and families. <div eID="gen15205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15206" type="x-p"/> 6. The Common People. <div eID="gen15206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15207" type="x-p"/> Those who disturb this natural order (for it subsists even in Britain) are enemies to the peace of the whole, whatever they may pretend to the contrary.
entries.f738f49f3a006998db54e4297cd649706d3c0e8d: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen15207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15208" type="x-p"/> Neither have our kings - In this verse he acknowledges that the kings, princes, priests, and fathers, had broken the law: but the prophets are left out; for they continued faithful to God, testifying by his Spirit against the crimes of all; and this even at the risk of their lives.
entries.a12b45c0f23210224a6538844bda6bf71d92650c: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen15208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15209" type="x-p"/> For they have not served thee in their kingdom - Instead of במלכותם bemalcutham, "in Their kingdom," במלכותך bemalcuthecha, in Thy kingdom," is the reading of two of Kennicott's MSS.; as also of the Septuagint, Syriac, and Arabic. This is most likely to be the true reading.
entries.02ce320e6b2d03d729175879e13d769724118e8a: <hi type="bold">Verse 36</hi> <div eID="gen15209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15210" type="x-p"/> Behold, we are servants - They had no king of their own: and were under the government of the kings of Persia, to whom they paid a regular tribute.
entries.74002d9d267770897322504f221dd5b26bac5f58: <hi type="bold">Verse 37</hi> <div eID="gen15210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15211" type="x-p"/> It yieldeth much increase unto the kings - Good and fruitful as the land is, yet it profits us little; as the chief profits on all things go to the kings of Persia. <div eID="gen15211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15212" type="x-p"/> Over our bodies - Exacting personal and feudal services from us, and from our cattle; and this not by any fixed rate, or rule, of so much rent, so much labor, or boons; but at their pleasure; so that we can neither call our persons, our time, our land, nor our cattle, our own: therefore we are in great distress. Miserable are the people that live under such a government. <div eID="gen15212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15213" type="x-p"/> Think of this, ye Britons! think of your liberties and rights. Compare them with any other nation under heaven, and see what a balance is in your favor. Almost all the nations of the earth acknowledge Britons the most happy of all men. May I not say, <div eID="gen15213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15214" type="x-p"/> O fortunatos nimium, sua si bona norint! "How exceedingly happy would you be, could you but consider your many advantages!"
entries.654ec26ad7ef184e8bc4b80dbd9f87094eadf095: <hi type="bold">Verse 38</hi> <div eID="gen15214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15215" type="x-p"/> Our princes, Levites, and priests, seal unto it - Persuaded that we have brought all the miseries upon ourselves by our transgressions, feeling much and fearing more, we make a covenant with thee to devote ourselves to thy service; to do with us as thou pleasest. From this sealing we learn that at this time the government of the Jews was a mixed aristocracy; composed of the nobles for the civil department, and the priests and Levites for the ecclesiastical. <div eID="gen15215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15216" type="x-p"/> This was not mixing the Church with the state, or the state with the Church: both were separate, yet both mutually supported each other. The state never attempted to model the Church according to its own mind; because the Church had been founded and regulated by God, and neither its creed nor its ordinances could be changed. The Church did not meddle with the state, to give it new laws, new ordinances, or new officers. Therefore the one could not be jealous of the other. Where this state of things prevails, every public blessing may be expected. In every state God says to the governors and the governed: "Render to Caesar the things which are Caesar's, and to God the things which are God's."  <chapter eID="Neh.9"/> <div eID="gen15216" type="x-p"/>

entries.859cf8f4c744421a91e2c8ab86f48a6c1f679cad: <reference osisRef="Neh.9.1">Neh 9:1</reference> <div eID="gen6601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6602" type="x-p"/> On the twenty-second of Tishri was the Hazereth of the feast of tabernacles; on the twenty-fourth the congregation re-assembled in the temple, “with fasting and with sackcloths (penitential garments made of hair; see rem. <reference osisRef="Joel.1.8">Joe 1:8</reference>) and earth upon them,” i.e., spread upon their heads (<reference osisRef="1Sam.4.12">1Sa 4:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.2">2Sa 1:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.2.12">Job 2:12</reference>), - the external marks of deep mourning and heaviness of heart.
entries.0cf2a103d0414f6bb46e10e8e584a88f9e3f8aab: <reference osisRef="Neh.9.2">Neh 9:2</reference> “And the seed of Israel separated themselves from all strangers, and stood and confessed all their sins, and the iniquities of their fathers.” This separation from strangers does not specially relate to the dissolution of the marriages contracted with heathen women, nor to any measures taken that only Israelites should be admitted to this assembly (Bertheau). It was rather a voluntary renunciation of connection with the heathen, and of heathen customs.
entries.815bb6c7a25ea6340fe79366132e6080e0b6e9ea: <reference osisRef="Neh.9.3">Neh 9:3</reference> <div eID="gen6602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6603" type="x-p"/> And they stood up (i.e., remained standing) in their place (comp. <reference osisRef="Neh.8.7">Neh 8:7</reference>), and read in the book of the law of the Lord their God, i.e., listened to the reading of the law, a fourth part of the day (about three hours), and a fourth part (the next three hours) they confessed (made a confession of their sins), and worshipped the Lord their God. This confession and worship is more nearly described vv. 4-37.
entries.79b0651a66ba20e1966600cc1344025480da6db9: <reference osisRef="Neh.9.4-Neh.9.5">Neh 9:4-5</reference> <div eID="gen6603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6604" type="x-p"/> There stood upon the scaffold of the Levites, i.e., upon the platform erected for the Levites (comp. <reference osisRef="Neh.8.4">Neh 8:4</reference>), Jeshua and seven other Levites whose names are given, and they cried with a loud voice to God, and said to the assembled congregation, “Stand up, bless the Lord your God for ever and ever! and blessed be the name of Thy glory, which is exalted above all blessing and praise.” The repetition of the names of the Levites in <reference osisRef="Neh.9.5">Neh 9:5</reference> shows that this invitation to praise God is distinct from the crying to God with a loud voice of <reference osisRef="Neh.9.4">Neh 9:4</reference>, and seems to say that the Levites first cried to God, i.e., addressed to Him their confessions and supplications, and after having done so, called upon the congregation to worship God. Eight names of Levites being given in both verses, and five of these - Jeshua, Bani, Kadmiel, Shebaniah, and Sherebiah - being identical, the difference of the three others in the two verses - Bunni, Bani, and Chenani (<reference osisRef="Neh.9.4">Neh 9:4</reference>), and Hashabniah, Hodijah, and Pethahiah (<reference osisRef="Neh.9.5">Neh 9:5</reference>) - seems to have arisen from a clerical error, - an appearance favoured also by the circumstance that Bani occurs twice in Neh 9:4. Of the other names in question, Hodijah occurs <reference osisRef="Neh.10.14">Neh 10:14</reference>, and Pethahiah Ezr 10:23, as names of Levites, but כּנני and חשׁבניה nowhere else. Hence Bunni, Bani, and Chenani (<reference osisRef="Neh.9.4">Neh 9:4</reference>), and Hashabniah (<reference osisRef="Neh.9.5">Neh 9:5</reference>), may be assigned to a clerical error; but we have no means for restoring the correct names. With regard to the matter of these verses, Ramb. remarks on <reference osisRef="Neh.9.4">Neh 9:4</reference> : <hi type="italic">constitisse opinor omnes simul, ita tamen ut unus tantum eodem tempore fuerit precatus, ceteris ipsi adstantibus atque sua etiam vice Deum orantibus,</hi> hence that the eight Levites prayed to God successively; while Bertheau thinks that these Levites entreated God, in penitential and supplicatory psalms, to have mercy on His sinful but penitent people. In this case we must also regard their address to the congregation in <reference osisRef="Neh.9.5">Neh 9:5</reference> as a liturgical hymn, to which the congregation responded by praising God in chorus. To this view may be objected the circumstance, that no allusion is made in the narrative to the singing of penitential or other songs. Besides, a confession of sins follows in vv. 6-37, which may fitly be called a crying unto God, without its being stated by whom it was uttered. “This section,” says Bertheau, “whether we regard its form or contents, cannot have been sung either by the Levites or the congregation. We recognise in it the speech of an individual, and hence accept the view that the statement of the lxx, that after the singing of the Levites, <reference osisRef="Neh.9.4">Neh 9:4</reference>, and the praising of God in <reference osisRef="Neh.9.5">Neh 9:5</reference>, Ezra came forward and spoke the words following, is correct, and that the words καὶ εἶπεν Ἔσδρας, which it inserts before <reference osisRef="Neh.9.6">Neh 9:6</reference>, originally stood in the Hebrew text.” But if Psalms, such as Ps 105-106, and 107, were evidently appointed to be sung to the praise of God by the Levites or by the congregation, there can be no reason why the prayer vv. 6-37 should not be adapted both in form and matter for this purpose. This prayer by no means bears the impress of being the address of an individual, but is throughout the confession of the whole congregation. The prayer speaks of <hi type="italic">our</hi> fathers (<reference osisRef="Neh.9.9">Neh 9:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.9.16">Neh 9:16</reference>), of what is come upon <hi type="italic">us</hi> (<reference osisRef="Neh.9.33">Neh 9:33</reference>), addresses Jahve as <hi type="italic">our</hi> God, and says <hi type="italic">we</hi> have sinned. Of course Ezra might have uttered it in the name of the congregation; but that the addition of the lxx, καὶ εἶπεν Ἔσδρας, is of no critical value, and is a mere conjecture of the translators, is evident from the circumstance that the prayer does not begin with the words יהוה הוּא אתּה of v. 6, but passes into the form of direct address to God in the last clause of v. 5: Blessed be the name of <hi type="italic">Thy</hi> glory. By these words the prayer which follows is evidently declared to be the confession of those who are to praise the glory of the Lord; and the addition, “and Ezra said,” characterized as an unskilful interpolation. <div eID="gen6604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6605" type="x-p"/> According to what has now been said, the summons, יהוה את בּרכוּ קוּמוּ, <reference osisRef="Neh.9.5">Neh 9:5</reference>, like the introductions to may Hodu and Hallelujah Psalms (e.g., <reference osisRef="Ps.105.1">Psa 105:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.106.1">Psa 106:1</reference>), is to be regarded as only an exhortation to the congregation to praise God, i.e., to join in the praises following, and to unite heartily in the confession of sin. This view of the connection of <reference osisRef="Neh.9.5">Neh 9:5</reference> and <reference osisRef="Neh.9.6">Neh 9:6</reference> explains the reason why it is not stated either in <reference osisRef="Neh.9.6">Neh 9:6</reference>, or at the close of this prayer in <reference osisRef="Neh.9.37">Neh 9:37</reference>, that the assembled congregation blessed God agreeably to the summons thus addressed to them. They did so by silently and heartily praying to, and praising God with the Levites, who were reciting aloud the confession of sin. On ויברכוּ R. Sal. already remarks: <hi type="italic">nunc incipiunt loqui Levitae versus Shechinam s. ad ipsum Deum</hi>. The invitation to praise God insensibly passes into the action of praising. If, moreover, vv. 6-37 are related in the manner above stated to <reference osisRef="Neh.9.5">Neh 9:5</reference>, then it is not probable that the crying to God with a loud voice (<reference osisRef="Neh.9.4">Neh 9:4</reference>) was anything else than the utterance of the prayer subsequently given, vv. 6-37. The repetition of the names in <reference osisRef="Neh.9.5">Neh 9:5</reference> is not enough to confirm this view, but must be explained by the breadth of the representation here given, and is rescued from the charge of mere tautology by the fact that in <reference osisRef="Neh.9.4">Neh 9:4</reference> the office of the individuals in question is not named, which it is by the word הלויּם in Neh 9:5. For הלויּם in <reference osisRef="Neh.9.4">Neh 9:4</reference> belongs as genitive to מעלה, and both priests and laymen might have stood on the platform of the Levites. For this reason it is subsequently stated in <reference osisRef="Neh.9.5">Neh 9:5</reference>, that Jeshua, etc., were Levites; and in doing this the names are again enumerated. In the exhortation, Stand up and bless, etc., Bertheau seeks to separate “for ever and ever” from the imp. בּרכוּ, and to take it as a further qualification of אלהיכם. This is, however, unnatural and arbitrary; comp. 1Ch 16:26. Still more arbitrary is it to supply “One day all people” to ויברכוּ, “shall bless Thy name,” etc. וגו וּמרומם adds a second predicate to שׁם: and which is exalted above all blessing and praise, i.e., <hi type="italic">sublimius est quam ut pro dignitate laudari possit</hi> (R. Sal.). <div eID="gen6605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6606" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Neh.9.6">Neh 9:6</reference> this praising of God begins with the acknowledgment that Jahve, the Creator of heaven and earth, chose Abram and made a covenant with him to give the land of Canaan to his seed, and had performed this word (<reference osisRef="Neh.9.6-Neh.9.8">Neh 9:6-8</reference>). These verses form the theme of that blessing the name of His glory, to which the Levites exhorted. This theme is then elucidated by facts from Israel’s history, in four strophes. <hi type="italic">a</hi>. When God saw the affliction of His people in Egypt, He delivered them by great signs and wonders from the power of Pharaoh, gave them laws and judgments on Sinai, miraculously provided them with food and water in the wilderness, and commanded them to take possession of the promised land (<reference osisRef="Neh.9.9-Neh.9.15">Neh 9:9-15</reference>). <hi type="italic">b</hi>. Although their fathers rebelled against Him, even in the wilderness, God did not withdraw His mercy from them, but sustained them forty years, so that they lacked nothing; and subdued kings before them, so that they were able to conquer and possess the land (<reference osisRef="Neh.9.16-Neh.9.25">Neh 9:16-25</reference>). <hi type="italic">c</hi>. After they were settled in the land they rebelled again, and God delivered them into the hand of their oppressors; but as often as they cried unto Him, He helped them again, till at length, because of their continued opposition, He gave them into the power of the people of the lands, yet of His great mercy did not wholly cast them off (<reference osisRef="Neh.9.26-Neh.9.31">Neh 9:26-31</reference>). <hi type="italic">d</hi>. May He now too look upon the affliction of His people, as the God that keepeth covenant and mercy, although they have deserved by their sins the troubles they are suffering (<reference osisRef="Neh.9.32-Neh.9.37">Neh 9:32-37</reference>).  “Thou art Jahve alone; Thou hast made heaven, the heaven of heavens, and all their host, the earth and all that is thereon, the sea and all therein; and Thou givest life to them all, and the host of heaven worshippeth Thee. <reference osisRef="Neh.9.7">Neh 9:7</reference> Thou art Jahve, the God who didst choose Abram, and broughtest him forth out of Ur of the Chaldees, and gavest him the name of Abraham: <reference osisRef="Neh.9.8">Neh 9:8</reference> And foundest his heart faithful before Thee, and madest a covenant with him to give the land of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, and the Perizzites, and the Jebusites, and the Girgashites, to give to his seed, and hast performed Thy word; for Thou art righteous.” Jahve alone is God, the Creator of heaven and earth, and of all creatures in heaven and on earth. In order duly to exalt the almightiness of God, the notion of heaven is enhanced by the addition “heaven of heavens,” as in <reference osisRef="Deut.10.14">Deu 10:14</reference>; 1Ki 8:27; and that of earth by the addition ”the sea and all therein;” comp. Psa 146:6. כּל־צבאם, <reference osisRef="Gen.2.1">Gen 2:1</reference>, here refers only to heaven. מחיּה, to cause to live = to give and preserve life. כּלּם relates to all creatures in heaven and earth. The host of heaven who worshipped God are the angels, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.148.2">Psa 148:2</reference>; Psa 103:21. This only God chose Abram; comp. <reference osisRef="Gen.12.1">Gen 12:1</reference> with <reference osisRef="Gen.11.31">Gen 11:31</reference> and <reference osisRef="Gen.15.7">Gen 15:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.17.5">Gen 17:5</reference>, where God bestowed upon the patriarch Abram the name of Abraham. The words, “Thou foundest his heart faithful,” refer to בּיהוה האמין there mentioned. The making of a covenant alludes to Gen 17:5.; the enumeration of six Canaanitish nations to <reference osisRef="Deut.7.1">Deu 7:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.3.8">Exo 3:8</reference>; comp. with Gen 15:20. This His word God performed (fulfilled), for He is righteous. God is called צדּיק, inasmuch as with Him word and deed correspond with each other; comp. Deu 32:4. <div eID="gen6606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6607" type="x-p"/> The fulfilment of this word by the deliverance of Israel from Egypt, and their guidance through the wilderness to Canaan.
